entry.title: Swift Package Manager: A Practical Guide

link.title: Swift Package Manager: A Practical Guide

entry.content:
Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) is the official tool for building, sharing, and depending on Swift code. It’s part of the Swift toolchain and built into Xcode, needs no extra installation, and has become the default way to add libraries to Apple-platform projects. It’s also the best tool for splitting your own app into modules. This guide goes past “paste a URL into Xcode”: we’ll build a real multi-target package with resources, a local dependency, a code-generating build plugin, and Swift Testing tests, then look at how version resolution works, how to modularize an app, and the mistakes that cause most SwiftPM headaches.

Swift Package Manager: A Practical Guide

Packages, targets, and products

Three words, often confused:

  • A package is a folder with a Package.swift manifest and source code. It’s the unit of versioning and distribution: one Git repository, one set of version tags.
  • A target is a unit of compilation: one module. Sources/GreetingCore/ becomes the GreetingCore module, which other code imports. Test targets live in Tests/.
  • A product is what the package offers to others: a library (made of one or more targets) or an executable. Targets that aren’t part of any product are internal to the package.

Clients depend on packages and link products; inside a package, targets depend on each other directly.

Creating a package

From the terminal:

mkdir Greeting && cd Greeting
swift package init --type library     # also: executable, tool, macro, build-tool-plugin…
swift build
swift test

Or in Xcode: File → New → Package. Opening the folder (or Package.swift) in Xcode works too: there’s no project file to maintain, because the manifest is the project.

A real package, end to end

Here’s the layout of the package we’ll build. It has a core module with a JSON resource, a public library that depends on another package, a command-line tool, a build plugin that generates source code, and tests:

Greeting/
├── Package.swift
├── Sources/
│   ├── GreetingCore/
│   │   ├── Greetings.swift
│   │   └── Resources/greetings.json
│   ├── Greeting/Greeting.swift
│   ├── greet/main.swift
│   └── VersionGen/main.swift
├── Plugins/
│   └── VersionPlugin/VersionPlugin.swift
└── Tests/
    └── GreetingCoreTests/GreetingTableTests.swift

The manifest

Package.swift is ordinary Swift code that uses the PackageDescription API:

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "Greeting",
    defaultLocalization: "en",
    platforms: [.macOS(.v13), .iOS(.v16)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "Greeting", targets: ["Greeting"]),
        .executable(name: "greet", targets: ["greet"]),
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(path: "../Formatting"),
        // A remote dependency looks like this:
        // .package(url: "https://github.com/apple/swift-collections.git", from: "1.1.0"),
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "GreetingCore",
            resources: [.process("Resources")],
            plugins: [.plugin(name: "VersionPlugin")]
        ),
        .target(
            name: "Greeting",
            dependencies: [
                "GreetingCore",
                .product(name: "Formatting", package: "Formatting"),
            ]
        ),
        .executableTarget(name: "greet", dependencies: ["Greeting"]),
        .executableTarget(name: "VersionGen"),
        .plugin(name: "VersionPlugin", capability: .buildTool(), dependencies: ["VersionGen"]),
        .testTarget(name: "GreetingCoreTests", dependencies: ["GreetingCore"]),
    ]
)

A few things worth knowing about this file:

  • The first line isn’t a normal comment. // swift-tools-version: 6.0 is required, and it selects the manifest API you can use and the minimum SwiftPM version that can build the package. With 6.0 and later, it also makes Swift 6 language mode the default for every target.
  • platforms sets minimum deployment targets. Without it, SwiftPM assumes very old OS versions, and APIs like Task or Bundle.module features will fail to compile with “only available in macOS 10.15 or newer” errors.
  • Only the Greeting library is a product. GreetingCore is an internal building block that clients can’t link directly.
  • Remote dependencies are referenced by URL, local ones by path. A local path dependency is ideal while developing two packages side by side.

Resources and Bundle.module

Code can’t assume where resource files end up: inside an app bundle, a test bundle, or next to a command-line tool. SwiftPM solves that by generating a Bundle.module accessor for any target with resources:

// Sources/GreetingCore/Greetings.swift
import Foundation

package struct GreetingTable: Sendable {
    package let entries: [String: String]

    package init() throws {
        let url = Bundle.module.url(forResource: "greetings", withExtension: "json")!
        entries = try JSONDecoder().decode([String: String].self, from: Data(contentsOf: url))
    }

    package func word(for language: String) -> String {
        entries[language] ?? entries["en", default: "Hi"]
    }
}

.process("Resources") lets SwiftPM optimize files for the platform: asset catalogs are compiled, storyboards built, and .lproj folders treated as localizations (which is why defaultLocalization is set). .copy("Resources") keeps a folder exactly as it is, including its structure, which is what you want for something like a bundled website or a folder of fixtures.

Notice the package access level (Swift 5.9). GreetingTable is visible to every target in this package, Greeting included, but invisible to clients. Before package existed, the only options were public, which leaks implementation details to everyone, or @_spi and other workarounds. See Access Control in Swift for the full picture.

The library and the tool

// Sources/Greeting/Greeting.swift
import Formatting
import GreetingCore

public func greet(_ name: String, language: String = "en", loud: Bool = false) throws -> String {
    let text = "\(try GreetingTable().word(for: language)), \(name)"
    return loud ? shout(text) : text
}

public let greetingLibraryVersion = GreetingCore.libraryVersion

// Sources/greet/main.swift
import Greeting

print(try greet("Sam"))
print(try greet("Sam", language: "fr", loud: true))
print("built with Greeting \(greetingLibraryVersion)")

shout(_:) comes from the Formatting package. libraryVersion doesn’t appear in any source file you’ve seen so far: the build plugin generates it.

A build tool plugin

Build tool plugins run during every build, and generate source files or resources that get compiled into the target, which is how tools like SwiftGen and protocol buffer generators integrate. A plugin is a small Swift program that tells SwiftPM which commands to run; the actual work is done by an executable target, here VersionGen:

// Sources/VersionGen/main.swift
import Foundation

let output = CommandLine.arguments[1]
let source = "package let libraryVersion = \"1.4.0\"\n"
try source.write(toFile: output, atomically: true, encoding: .utf8)

// Plugins/VersionPlugin/VersionPlugin.swift
import PackagePlugin

@main
struct VersionPlugin: BuildToolPlugin {
    func createBuildCommands(context: PluginContext, target: Target) throws -> [Command] {
        let output = context.pluginWorkDirectoryURL.appending(path: "Version.swift")
        return [
            .buildCommand(
                displayName: "Generating Version.swift",
                executable: try context.tool(named: "VersionGen").url,
                arguments: [output.path()],
                outputFiles: [output]
            ),
        ]
    }
}

Because the command declares its output files, SwiftPM compiles the generated Version.swift into GreetingCore, and only reruns the generator when needed. Plugins run in a sandbox with no network access and write access only to their work directory, so a dependency’s plugin can’t quietly modify your source tree. Xcode also asks you to trust a package’s plugins (and macros) the first time you use them.

The other kind, command plugins, run on demand, for tasks like formatting or generating documentation: swift package plugin <name>, or right-clicking the package in Xcode. These may ask for permission to write to the package directory.

Tests with Swift Testing

Since Swift 6, the toolchain includes Swift Testing, with @Test functions, #expect, and parameterized tests:

// Tests/GreetingCoreTests/GreetingTableTests.swift
import Testing
@testable import GreetingCore

@Test func fallsBackToEnglish() throws {
    let table = try GreetingTable()
    #expect(table.word(for: "de") == "Hello")
}

@Test(arguments: ["en", "fr"])
func knownLanguages(language: String) throws {
    #expect(try GreetingTable().entries[language] != nil)
}

XCTest still works side by side, and swift test runs both.

Building, running, and testing

$ swift run greet
Hello, Sam
BONJOUR, SAM!
built with Greeting 1.4.0

$ swift test
✔ Test fallsBackToEnglish() passed after 0.005 seconds.
✔ Test knownLanguages(language:) with 2 test cases passed after 0.005 seconds.
✔ Test run with 2 tests in 0 suites passed after 0.005 seconds.

The JSON resource was found through Bundle.module, shout came from the other package, and the version string came from code that only exists in the build directory.

Versions and resolution

SwiftPM uses semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, read from the Git tags of each dependency. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for fixes. The requirement you write decides which versions are acceptable:

Requirement Accepts
from: "1.1.0" 1.1.0 up to, but not including, 2.0.0 (the usual choice)
.upToNextMinor(from: "1.1.0") 1.1.x only
exact: "1.1.3" exactly that version (avoid in libraries)
"1.1.0"..<"1.5.0" an explicit range
branch: "main" / revision: "…" a branch or commit (for development only)

SwiftPM resolves the whole graph at once, finding one version of each package that satisfies every requirement, from your manifest and from your dependencies’ manifests. There’s only one version of each package in a build; if two dependencies need incompatible ranges of the same package, resolution fails, and the error lists the conflicting requirements. That’s the strongest argument for libraries using broad ranges like from:, and never exact:.

The result is written to Package.resolved:

  • Commit it for apps (and for Xcode projects, where it lives inside the .xcodeproj or .xcworkspace), so every developer and CI machine builds exactly the same versions.
  • Libraries usually don’t commit it: their clients resolve their own graph anyway.
  • swift package update (or File → Packages → Update to Latest Package Versions) moves to the newest allowed versions; swift package resolve installs exactly what Package.resolved says.

Branch and revision dependencies are fine during development, but a package that depends on a branch can’t be depended on by version. Tag a release first.

Adding packages to an app

In Xcode: File → Add Package Dependencies…, paste the repository URL, pick a version rule, and choose which products to link to which targets. Xcode stores the dependency in the project file rather than in a Package.swift.

From the command line (Swift 6), swift package add-dependency <url> --from 1.1.0 edits a manifest for you, and add-target and add-product exist for the other common edits.

Modularizing your own app

Packages aren’t just for third-party code. Splitting an app into local packages, like Networking, DesignSystem, FeatureProfile, and a thin app target that wires them together, brings real benefits:

  • Faster incremental builds: an unchanged module isn’t recompiled, and modules that don’t depend on each other build in parallel.
  • Enforced boundaries: a feature module can only use what another module declares public, so accidental coupling becomes a compile error instead of a code review comment.
  • Fast tests: each module’s tests run on its own, often without launching the app or a simulator.
  • Faster SwiftUI previews, which build only the module you’re working on.

A common structure is one package with many targets, kept in the app’s repository:

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
// AppModules/Package.swift
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "AppModules",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "FeatureProfile", targets: ["FeatureProfile"]),
        .library(name: "FeatureSettings", targets: ["FeatureSettings"]),
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "Networking"),
        .target(name: "DesignSystem"),
        .target(name: "FeatureProfile", dependencies: ["Networking", "DesignSystem"]),
        .target(name: "FeatureSettings", dependencies: ["DesignSystem"]),
        .testTarget(name: "FeatureProfileTests", dependencies: ["FeatureProfile"]),
    ]
)

Drag the folder into your Xcode project, then link the feature products to the app target. Keep dependencies pointing one way, features depend on infrastructure, never the reverse and never feature-to-feature, and SwiftPM will reject cycles for you.

Swift settings per target

Targets can opt into compiler features and language modes individually, which is exactly what a gradual Swift 6 migration needs:

// .target(
//     name: "LegacyNetworking",
//     swiftSettings: [
//         .swiftLanguageMode(.v5),                          // stay in Swift 5 mode for now
//         .enableUpcomingFeature("StrictConcurrency"),       // but get concurrency warnings
//     ]
// ),
// .target(
//     name: "CppBridge",
//     swiftSettings: [.interoperabilityMode(.Cxx)]          // see the interop article
// ),

.define("FEATURE_X") adds a compilation condition for #if FEATURE_X, and condition: .when(platforms: [.iOS]) limits a setting or a dependency to some platforms. Avoid unsafeFlags: a package that uses them can’t be used as a versioned dependency by others. See Swift Interoperability for .interoperabilityMode(.Cxx).

Binary targets and macros

  • Binary targets distribute closed-source code as an XCFramework: .binaryTarget(name: "Analytics", url: "https://…/Analytics.xcframework.zip", checksum: "…"). Compute the checksum with swift package compute-checksum; SwiftPM refuses a download that doesn’t match it.
  • Macros are distributed as packages, with a .macro target holding the compiler plugin; see Macros in Swift. Because they depend on SwiftSyntax, they noticeably increase clean build times.

Useful commands

swift build -c release              # optimized build
swift test --parallel               # run tests in parallel
swift test --filter GreetingCoreTests
swift run greet                     # build and run an executable product
swift package resolve               # install exactly what Package.resolved says
swift package update                # move to the newest allowed versions
swift package show-dependencies     # print the resolved dependency tree
swift package describe              # print targets, products, and their sources
swift package clean                 # remove build artifacts
swift package reset                 # also remove the dependency cache

When resolution gets stuck in Xcode, File → Packages → Reset Package Caches is the equivalent of reset, and deleting DerivedData is the last resort.

Common pitfalls

  • Missing platforms, so availability errors appear for APIs your app clearly supports.
  • Loading resources with Bundle.main inside a package; use Bundle.module.
  • Overly strict requirements (exact:) in libraries, which cause resolution conflicts for everyone downstream.
  • Not committing Package.resolved in an app, so CI and teammates silently build different versions.
  • Making everything public to share code between targets; use package instead.
  • A single giant module, which throws away most of the build-time and boundary benefits.

Interview questions

What’s the difference between a target and a product? A target is a module that gets compiled; a product is what a package exposes to clients, made of one or more targets. Clients can only use products.

What does swift-tools-version control? The manifest API available, the minimum SwiftPM version that can build the package, and, from 6.0, the default Swift language mode.

Should Package.resolved be committed? For apps, yes, to get reproducible builds. Libraries usually don’t, since their clients resolve the whole graph themselves.

What happens if two dependencies need incompatible versions of the same package? Resolution fails: a build contains exactly one version of each package. That’s why libraries should use broad version ranges.

How do you share code between modules of one package without making it public? Use the package access level.

Summary

  • A package is versioned and distributed as a unit; targets are modules; products are what clients can use.
  • The manifest is Swift code; swift-tools-version and platforms matter more than they look.
  • Resources go through Bundle.module; package access shares code between targets without leaking it.
  • Build tool plugins generate code during the build, in a sandbox; Swift Testing comes with the toolchain.
  • One version of each package per build: use broad version ranges in libraries, and commit Package.resolved for apps.
  • Local packages are the most practical way to modularize an app, with per-target settings for gradual Swift 6 migration.
entry.summary: Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) is the official tool for building, sharing, and depending on Swift code. It’s part of the Swift toolchain and built into Xcode, needs no extra installation, and has become the default way to add libraries to Apple-platform projects. It’s also the best tool for splitting your own app into modules. This guide goes past “paste a URL into Xcode”: we’ll build a real multi-target package with resources, a local dependency, a code-generating build plugin, and Swift Testing tests, then look at how version resolution works, how to modularize an app, and the mistakes that cause most SwiftPM headaches.

entry.title: Operation and OperationQueue in Swift
entry.content:
Before async/await, Apple platforms offered two main ways to run work concurrently: Grand Central Dispatch for lightweight blocks, and Operation with OperationQueue for work that needed dependencies, cancellation, priorities, and limits on concurrency. Operations are built on top of GCD and still power many large codebases, and some of their ideas, like a dependency graph between units of work, have no direct one-line equivalent in Swift concurrency. This article covers how operations really behave, including the parts the documentation glosses over: cancelled dependencies, asynchronous operations and their KVO contract, passing data between operations, and bridging to async/await.

Operation and OperationQueue in Swift

The model in one paragraph

An Operation is an object that represents one unit of work and goes through a state machine: pending → ready → executing → finished, with cancelled as a flag that can be set at any time. An OperationQueue holds operations and starts each one when it becomes ready (all its dependencies have finished), running it on a thread from a GCD-managed pool. Because operations are objects, you can keep references to them, cancel them, inspect their state, observe them with KVO, and wire them together, which is what separates them from fire-and-forget GCD blocks.

The examples below record events through a small thread-safe helper, so their output is deterministic:

import Foundation

final class EventLog: @unchecked Sendable {
    private let lock = NSLock()
    private var storage: [String] = []

    func record(_ event: String) {
        lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }
        storage.append(event)
    }

    var events: [String] {
        lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }
        return storage
    }
}

The basics

The simplest operation is a block. addOperation(_:) with a closure wraps it in a BlockOperation for you:

let basicLog = EventLog()
let queue = OperationQueue()
queue.name = "com.example.images"     // shows up in the debugger and in crash logs
queue.maxConcurrentOperationCount = 2  // at most two operations at a time

queue.addOperation {
    basicLog.record("resize")
}

let compress = BlockOperation {
    basicLog.record("compress")
}
queue.addOperation(compress)
queue.waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished()
print(basicLog.events.sorted())   // ["compress", "resize"]

The order of those two isn’t guaranteed: with a concurrency limit of 2, they run at the same time. Setting maxConcurrentOperationCount = 1 makes the queue serial, but note that a serial OperationQueue still respects dependencies and priorities, so it’s not strictly first-in, first-out like a serial DispatchQueue.

A BlockOperation can hold several blocks with addExecutionBlock(_:). They run concurrently with each other, and the operation finishes only when all of them have finished.

Concurrency limits actually hold

maxConcurrentOperationCount is the feature people miss most when they move to other APIs. Here, six operations each take 20 ms, and we measure the highest number running at once:

final class Gauge: @unchecked Sendable {
    private let lock = NSLock()
    private var current = 0
    private(set) var peak = 0

    func enter() {
        lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }
        current += 1
        peak = max(peak, current)
    }

    func leave() {
        lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }
        current -= 1
    }
}

let gauge = Gauge()
let limitedQueue = OperationQueue()
limitedQueue.maxConcurrentOperationCount = 2

for _ in 1...6 {
    limitedQueue.addOperation {
        gauge.enter()
        Thread.sleep(forTimeInterval: 0.02)
        gauge.leave()
    }
}
limitedQueue.waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished()
print(gauge.peak)   // 2

That’s exactly what you want for “at most 3 downloads at a time” or “don’t decode more than 2 large images at once to limit memory”.

Dependencies

An operation doesn’t start until all of its dependencies have finished, even if they’re on different queues:

let pipelineLog = EventLog()
let download = BlockOperation { pipelineLog.record("download") }
let decode = BlockOperation { pipelineLog.record("decode") }
let save = BlockOperation { pipelineLog.record("save") }

decode.addDependency(download)
save.addDependency(decode)

let workQueue = OperationQueue()
workQueue.addOperations([save, decode, download], waitUntilFinished: true)
print(pipelineLog.events)   // ["download", "decode", "save"]

The operations were added in reverse order, and the queue could run three at once, but the dependencies forced the order.

Dependencies aren’t limited to chains. An operation can depend on several others, which makes fan-in easy: start ten downloads in parallel, and run a “build the gallery” operation that depends on all ten.

Two things to watch:

  • Cycles deadlock silently. If A depends on B and B depends on A, neither ever becomes ready, and nothing reports an error.
  • Add dependencies before adding operations to a queue. Adding them afterwards works only while the operation hasn’t started yet, which is a race.

Cancelled dependencies don’t stop dependents

This surprises almost everyone. “Finished” includes “finished because it was cancelled”, so a dependent operation still runs when its dependency was cancelled:

let cancelLog = EventLog()
let fetch = BlockOperation { cancelLog.record("fetch") }
let render = BlockOperation { cancelLog.record("render") }
render.addDependency(fetch)

fetch.cancel()

let cancelQueue = OperationQueue()
cancelQueue.addOperations([fetch, render], waitUntilFinished: true)
print(cancelLog.events)   // ["render"]

fetch never ran its block, yet render ran anyway, probably with missing data. The dependent operation must check its dependencies itself, for example if dependencies.contains(where: \.isCancelled) { return } at the top of main(), or you cancel the whole chain together with cancelAllOperations().

Cancellation is cooperative

Calling cancel() only sets a flag. An operation that hasn’t started yet will still be started by the queue, but the default start() sees the flag and finishes immediately, without calling main(). An operation that’s already running must check isCancelled itself:

final class ThumbnailOperation: Operation, @unchecked Sendable {
    let imageIDs: [Int]
    private(set) var processed = 0

    init(imageIDs: [Int]) {
        self.imageIDs = imageIDs
    }

    override func main() {
        for _ in imageIDs {
            if isCancelled { return }      // stop promptly when cancelled
            Thread.sleep(forTimeInterval: 0.001)
            processed += 1
        }
    }
}

let thumbnails = ThumbnailOperation(imageIDs: Array(1...1_000))
let thumbnailQueue = OperationQueue()
thumbnailQueue.addOperation(thumbnails)
Thread.sleep(forTimeInterval: 0.05)
thumbnails.cancel()
thumbnailQueue.waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished()
print(thumbnails.processed < 1_000, thumbnails.isCancelled, thumbnails.isFinished)   // true true true

Subclassing Operation and overriding main() is the standard way to write reusable, testable units of work. @unchecked Sendable acknowledges that Operation subclasses manage their own thread safety, which Swift 6’s checker can’t verify. That’s a real promise: here, processed is only written by the operation itself and read after it has finished, so it’s safe.

Checking isCancelled once per loop iteration, or between stages, is usually enough. Checking only at the start of main() isn’t: an operation cancelled mid-way would run to completion.

Passing data between operations

Operations have no built-in return value. The idiomatic way to pass results is through the dependency: the consumer looks up its producer, which is guaranteed to have finished:

final class FetchNumbers: Operation, @unchecked Sendable {
    private(set) var output: [Int] = []

    override func main() {
        guard !isCancelled else { return }
        output = [3, 1, 2]
    }
}

final class SumNumbers: Operation, @unchecked Sendable {
    private(set) var total: Int?

    override func main() {
        guard let input = dependencies.compactMap({ $0 as? FetchNumbers }).first,
              !input.isCancelled else { return }
        total = input.output.reduce(0, +)
    }
}

let fetchNumbers = FetchNumbers()
let sumNumbers = SumNumbers()
sumNumbers.addDependency(fetchNumbers)

OperationQueue().addOperations([fetchNumbers, sumNumbers], waitUntilFinished: true)
print(sumNumbers.total ?? -1)   // 6

Because the dependency has finished before main() runs, reading output doesn’t race. This also handles the cancelled-dependency problem from earlier: SumNumbers refuses to run on missing data. An alternative is an “adapter” BlockOperation between the two that copies the output across, which keeps each operation unaware of the other’s type.

Asynchronous operations

By default, an operation is finished as soon as main() returns. That’s wrong for work that completes later, like a network request with a completion handler: the queue would consider it done immediately, start its dependents too early, and stop counting it toward the concurrency limit.

An asynchronous operation overrides start() and manages its own state, and must send KVO notifications for isExecuting and isFinished, because that’s how the queue learns about state changes. Here’s a reusable base class:

class AsyncOperation: Operation, @unchecked Sendable {
    private enum State {
        case ready, executing, finished
    }

    private let stateLock = NSLock()
    private var _state = State.ready

    private var state: State {
        get {
            stateLock.lock(); defer { stateLock.unlock() }
            return _state
        }
        set {
            willChangeValue(forKey: "isExecuting")
            willChangeValue(forKey: "isFinished")
            stateLock.lock()
            _state = newValue
            stateLock.unlock()
            didChangeValue(forKey: "isFinished")
            didChangeValue(forKey: "isExecuting")
        }
    }

    override var isAsynchronous: Bool { true }
    override var isExecuting: Bool { state == .executing }
    override var isFinished: Bool { state == .finished }

    override func start() {
        if isCancelled {
            state = .finished
            return
        }
        state = .executing
        execute()
    }

    /// Subclasses do their work here and must call `finish()` exactly once.
    func execute() {
        fatalError("Subclasses must override execute()")
    }

    final func finish() {
        state = .finished
    }
}

final class DelayedGreeting: AsyncOperation, @unchecked Sendable {
    private(set) var message: String?

    override func execute() {
        DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 0.05) {
            self.message = "Hello after a delay"
            self.finish()
        }
    }
}

let greetingLog = EventLog()
let greeting = DelayedGreeting()
let afterGreeting = BlockOperation { greetingLog.record("dependent ran") }
afterGreeting.addDependency(greeting)

OperationQueue().addOperations([greeting, afterGreeting], waitUntilFinished: true)
print(greeting.message ?? "nil", greetingLog.events)   // Hello after a delay ["dependent ran"]

The details that make this correct:

  • KVO notifications are sent outside the lock. Observers (the queue) read isFinished from inside the notification; holding the lock there would deadlock.
  • start() checks for cancellation first, and moves to finished without doing any work, because the queue still calls start() on cancelled operations.
  • finish() must be called exactly once, on every path, including errors and cancellation. Forget it, and the operation never finishes: its dependents never run, and waitUntilFinished hangs forever.
  • Don’t call super.start() in an asynchronous operation; the default implementation would call main() and mark the operation finished when it returns.

This boilerplate, and how easy it is to get subtly wrong, is one of the main reasons people moved to Swift concurrency.

Completion blocks, barriers, and waiting

let reportLog = EventLog()
let report = BlockOperation { reportLog.record("build report") }
report.completionBlock = {
    reportLog.record("report finished")   // runs on a background thread
}

let reportQueue = OperationQueue()
reportQueue.addOperation(report)
reportQueue.addBarrierBlock {
    reportLog.record("barrier: everything before me is done")
}
reportQueue.waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished()
print(reportLog.events.first ?? "", reportLog.events.count)   // build report 3
  • completionBlock runs on an arbitrary thread once the operation finishes, even when it finished because it was cancelled. Hop to the main queue before touching UI, check isCancelled if it matters, and watch for retain cycles: a completion block stored on an operation that captures the operation strongly keeps it alive. The completion block runs concurrently with whatever the queue does next, so it isn’t ordered relative to dependents either.
  • addBarrierBlock(_:) (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15) runs a block after every operation added before it has finished, and holds back operations added after it, like a dispatch barrier.
  • waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished() and waitUntilFinished: true block the calling thread. Never call them on the main thread, and never inside Swift concurrency code, where blocking a cooperative pool thread can stall everything.

Priorities and quality of service

let urgent = BlockOperation { print("User is waiting for this") }
urgent.queuePriority = .high
urgent.qualityOfService = .userInitiated

let background = OperationQueue()
background.qualityOfService = .utility
  • queuePriority orders ready operations within one queue. It never overrides dependencies: a high-priority operation whose dependency hasn’t finished still waits.
  • qualityOfService tells the system how important the work is for CPU and energy scheduling. An operation’s QoS overrides its queue’s default, and the system raises a dependency’s QoS when a more urgent operation is waiting on it, which avoids priority inversion.

Suspending, observing, and progress

  • isSuspended = true stops a queue from starting new operations (running ones continue). It’s useful for pausing downloads when the app loses connectivity.
  • isExecuting, isFinished, isCancelled, isReady, and the queue’s operationCount are KVO-compliant, which is how progress UIs were traditionally built; see Key-Value Observing in Swift.
  • OperationQueue.progress (iOS 13): set progress.totalUnitCount before adding operations, and each finished operation counts as one unit, which you can attach to a UIProgressView via its observedProgress.

Bridging to async/await

Operations can’t be awaited directly, but a continuation turns “everything on this queue is done” into an await. A barrier block makes a convenient signal:

extension OperationQueue {
    func waitForAll() async {
        await withCheckedContinuation { (continuation: CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>) in
            addBarrierBlock {
                continuation.resume()
            }
        }
    }
}

let bridgeLog = EventLog()
let bridgeQueue = OperationQueue()
bridgeQueue.addOperation { bridgeLog.record("legacy work") }
await bridgeQueue.waitForAll()
print(bridgeLog.events)   // ["legacy work"]

Unlike waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished(), this suspends instead of blocking, so it’s safe to call from async code. In fact, the SDK enforces this: calling waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished(), addOperations(_:waitUntilFinished:) or Thread.sleep from an async context is a compile error (“unavailable from asynchronous contexts; Use addBarrierBlock or a dependent Operations instead”). It’s a handy seam when migrating an operation-based codebase to Swift concurrency one layer at a time.

Operations vs. GCD vs. Swift concurrency

Need Good fit
Fire off a quick block in the background GCD or a Task
A real dependency graph, with fan-out and fan-in OperationQueue
Limiting concurrency, e.g. at most 3 downloads OperationQueue, or a task group that adds a new child as each one finishes
Cancelling a whole tree of work, with errors propagating Swift concurrency (structured tasks)
Readable sequential async code async/await
Protecting shared mutable state actors

In new code, Swift concurrency covers most of what operations offered, with less ceremony and with compiler-checked data-race safety: task groups for parallel work, cancellation that propagates to children automatically, async let for simple dependencies. Operations remain a solid choice for explicit dependency graphs and in existing codebases built around them. See Swift Concurrency for the modern approach.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming a cancelled dependency stops its dependents. It doesn’t; check dependencies for cancellation.
  • Checking isCancelled only once, so long-running operations ignore cancellation.
  • Asynchronous operations that never call finish(), or that change state without KVO notifications. The queue hangs, silently.
  • Dependency cycles, which deadlock without any error.
  • Blocking waits on the main thread or in async code.
  • Retain cycles in completionBlock that capture the operation itself.
  • Mutable state shared between operations without synchronization. Operations run on many threads; @unchecked Sendable is a promise, not a protection.

Interview questions

What happens to an operation’s dependents when the operation is cancelled? They still run: a cancelled operation counts as finished. Dependents must check whether their dependencies were cancelled.

What’s the difference between overriding main() and overriding start()? Overriding main() gives a synchronous operation: it’s finished when main() returns. Overriding start() gives an asynchronous operation, which must manage isExecuting and isFinished itself, with KVO notifications, and finish exactly once.

How do you limit the number of concurrent tasks with OperationQueue? Set maxConcurrentOperationCount. A value of 1 makes the queue serial, while still respecting dependencies and priorities.

What’s the difference between queuePriority and qualityOfService? queuePriority orders ready operations within a queue; qualityOfService influences system-wide CPU and energy scheduling.

When would you still choose operations over Swift concurrency? For explicit, reusable dependency graphs, for strict concurrency limits with little code, and in codebases already built around operations.

Summary

  • OperationQueue runs Operation objects concurrently; maxConcurrentOperationCount limits how many run at once, and really does.
  • Dependencies order work across queues and allow fan-in, but cancelled dependencies still count as finished.
  • Cancellation is cooperative: check isCancelled regularly in main().
  • Pass data through dependencies; write asynchronous operations by overriding start() and sending KVO notifications for state changes.
  • Barriers, completion blocks, priorities, QoS, and progress round out the API; bridge to async/await with a continuation, and prefer Swift concurrency for new code.

entry.title: Swift Concurrency: async/await, Tasks, and Actors

link.title: Swift Concurrency: async/await, Tasks, and Actors

entry.content:
For years, asynchronous Swift meant completion handlers, nested closures, and manual hops between dispatch queues, with data races found only by luck or by Thread Sanitizer. Swift concurrency replaces that with features built into the language: async/await for code that reads top to bottom, tasks for running work concurrently with structured cancellation, actors for protecting shared state, and, since Swift 6, a compiler that proves your code is free of data races. This article is a tour of the whole model, including the parts that trip people up.

Swift Concurrency: async/await, Tasks, and Actors

async and await

A function marked async can suspend while it waits for something, without blocking a thread. Callers mark each potential suspension point with await:

struct Profile: Sendable {
    let name: String
}

func fetchProfile(id: Int) async throws -> Profile {
    try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(50))     // stand-in for a network call
    return Profile(name: "User \(id)")
}

func showProfile() async {
    do {
        let profile = try await fetchProfile(id: 42)
        print(profile.name)
    } catch {
        print("Failed: \(error)")
    }
}

Compare that with the completion-handler version: no nesting, normal do/catch error handling, no way to forget to call a completion handler on some path, and no way to call it twice.

Suspending is not blocking. While fetchProfile waits, the thread it was running on is free to run other work. When the result is ready, the function resumes, possibly on a different thread. Two consequences:

  • Code between two awaits runs without interruption, but anything can happen at an await. Other code may run and change state before you resume.
  • Don’t assume which thread you’re on after an await, unless you’re isolated to an actor (see below).

The cooperative thread pool

Swift concurrency runs tasks on a cooperative thread pool with roughly one thread per CPU core. Instead of creating a thread per piece of work (and paying for thread creation and context switches), tasks take turns: when one suspends, its thread picks up another task.

That design has one hard rule: never block a thread in async code. Waiting on a DispatchSemaphore, a DispatchGroup.wait(), or a lock held across long work keeps a pool thread busy doing nothing, and with only a handful of threads, a few blocked ones can stall the entire app. Always await instead.

Calling async code from sync code: Task

You can only await inside an async context. To start async work from synchronous code, like a button action, create a Task:

func buttonTapped() {
    Task {
        await showProfile()
    }
}

A Task { } created this way is unstructured: it runs independently, and you can keep a handle to it to cancel it or await its result (task.value). It also inherits the caller’s actor context and priority: a task created from main-actor UI code runs on the main actor, which is what you want for updating the UI. Task.detached { } inherits nothing, and is rarely needed.

Running work in parallel

await calls one after another, and they run sequentially. To run independent work at the same time, use async let:

func loadDashboard() async throws -> (Profile, Profile) {
    async let first = fetchProfile(id: 1)       // starts immediately
    async let second = fetchProfile(id: 2)      // also starts immediately
    return try await (first, second)            // wait for both
}

For a dynamic number of child tasks, use a task group. Results arrive in completion order, not the order the tasks were added:

func delayed(_ value: Int, milliseconds: Int) async throws -> Int {
    try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(milliseconds))
    return value
}

let completionOrder = try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Int.self) { group in
    group.addTask { try await delayed(1, milliseconds: 60) }
    group.addTask { try await delayed(2, milliseconds: 10) }
    group.addTask { try await delayed(3, milliseconds: 30) }

    var results: [Int] = []
    for try await value in group {
        results.append(value)
    }
    return results
}
print(completionOrder)   // [2, 3, 1]

If you need the original order, return the index along with each result and sort, or store results in a dictionary keyed by input.

This is structured concurrency: child tasks (from async let and task groups) can’t outlive the scope that created them. If one child throws, the group cancels the others; if the parent is cancelled, so are its children. That’s what makes concurrent code as predictable as sequential code.

Cancellation is cooperative

Cancelling a task sets a flag. Nothing is forcibly stopped: the task checks the flag at convenient points and decides how to stop. Many APIs check it for you: Task.sleep throws CancellationError when cancelled, and URLSession cancels the request:

let job = Task { () -> String in
    do {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(5))
        return "finished"
    } catch {
        return "cancelled: \(type(of: error))"
    }
}
job.cancel()
print(await job.value)   // cancelled: CancellationError

In your own long-running loops, check it yourself, with try Task.checkCancellation() (throws) or Task.isCancelled (a Bool):

func processLines(_ lines: [String]) async throws -> Int {
    var count = 0
    for line in lines {
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        count += line.count
    }
    return count
}

To react immediately, for example to cancel an underlying callback-based operation, use withTaskCancellationHandler.

Task-local values

@TaskLocal values flow automatically to child tasks, which is great for request IDs, tracing, and logging context:

enum RequestContext {
    @TaskLocal static var requestID = "none"
}

await RequestContext.$requestID.withValue("req-42") {
    await Task {
        print("child task sees \(RequestContext.requestID)")   // req-42
    }.value
}
print(RequestContext.requestID)   // none: the value only exists inside withValue

Actors: safe shared mutable state

A data race happens when two threads access the same memory at the same time and at least one writes. Actors prevent them: an actor’s mutable state can only be touched by one task at a time, and the compiler enforces that every access from outside goes through await:

actor BankAccount {
    private(set) var balance = 0

    func deposit(_ amount: Int) {
        balance += amount
    }

    func withdraw(_ amount: Int) -> Bool {
        guard balance >= amount else { return false }
        balance -= amount
        return true
    }
}

let account = BankAccount()
await account.deposit(100)          // `await`: we may have to wait our turn
let ok = await account.withdraw(30)
print(ok, await account.balance)    // true 70

Inside the actor, methods run one at a time, so no locks are needed. From outside, every access is awaited, because the actor might be busy with someone else.

Reentrancy: the actor trap

Actors run one call at a time, except at awaits. While an actor method is suspended, other calls to the actor can run. That makes actors deadlock-free, but it means state can change across a suspension point:

actor Wallet {
    private(set) var balance = 100

    private func authorize(_ amount: Int) async throws {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(10))   // e.g. a call to a payment server
    }

    func spendBroken(_ amount: Int) async throws -> Bool {
        guard balance >= amount else { return false }
        try await authorize(amount)          // suspension: another spend can run here!
        balance -= amount
        return true
    }

    func spendFixed(_ amount: Int) async throws -> Bool {
        guard balance >= amount else { return false }
        balance -= amount                    // change state before suspending...
        do {
            try await authorize(amount)
        } catch {
            balance += amount                // ...and roll back on failure
            throw error
        }
        return true
    }
}

let broken = Wallet()
async let firstSpend = broken.spendBroken(80)
async let secondSpend = broken.spendBroken(80)
print(try await [firstSpend, secondSpend], await broken.balance)   // [true, true] -60

let fixed = Wallet()
async let thirdSpend = fixed.spendFixed(80)
async let fourthSpend = fixed.spendFixed(80)
print(try await [thirdSpend, fourthSpend], await fixed.balance)    // [true, false] 20

Both broken calls passed the balance check before either one subtracted, so the wallet overdrew. The rule: don’t assume state is unchanged after an await inside an actor. Either update state before suspending, or re-check it afterwards.

The main actor

UI code must run on the main thread. @MainActor is a global actor that expresses that in the type system:

@MainActor
final class ProfileViewModel {
    var title = "Loading…"

    func load() async {
        do {
            let profile = try await fetchProfile(id: 7)   // runs off the main actor
            title = profile.name                          // back on the main actor
        } catch {
            title = "Error"
        }
    }
}

The compiler ensures title is only touched on the main actor, and await hops back automatically after the network call. No more DispatchQueue.main.async. Mark individual members nonisolated when they don’t need main-actor protection.

Sendable and Swift 6 data-race safety

Values that cross from one concurrency domain to another (into a task, into an actor, back to the main actor) must be safe to share. That’s what the Sendable protocol marks:

  • value types whose stored properties are all Sendable (inferred automatically for non-public structs and enums),
  • actors,
  • final classes with only immutable (let), Sendable properties,
  • classes that do their own synchronization, marked @unchecked Sendable (a promise the compiler can’t verify).

In Swift 6 language mode, these rules are enforced as errors: the compiler proves that your code has no data races. For example, sharing a mutable, non-Sendable object with a detached task is rejected, with an error saying that sending the closure risks causing data races:

final class Counter {
    var value = 0
}

func racy() {
    let counter = Counter()
    // Task.detached { counter.value += 1 }   // ❌ error in Swift 6: sending this closure risks data races
    counter.value += 1
}

Swift 6 also adds region-based isolation, which lets the compiler accept code that passes a non-Sendable value to another task when it can prove the original code never uses it again, and the sending keyword, which states that ownership of a value is transferred. Together, they remove many false alarms that made strict checking painful in earlier releases.

Migrating an existing project to Swift 6 mode can take work, but you can do it gradually: enable complete checking as warnings first, fix one module at a time, and switch modules to Swift 6 mode individually.

Bridging callbacks and delegates

Wrap a single-result completion handler with a continuation, which must be resumed exactly once:

func legacyFetch(completion: @escaping @Sendable (Result<String, Error>) -> Void) {
    completion(.success("data"))
}

func modernFetch() async throws -> String {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyFetch { result in
            continuation.resume(with: result)
        }
    }
}

The “checked” variant traps if you resume twice, and warns if you never resume. For a stream of values, like delegate callbacks or a sensor, use AsyncStream:

final class Sensor: @unchecked Sendable {
    var onReading: ((Double) -> Void)?
    func emit() { [1.5, 2.5].forEach { onReading?($0) } }
}

func readings(from sensor: Sensor) -> AsyncStream<Double> {
    AsyncStream { continuation in
        sensor.onReading = { continuation.yield($0) }
        continuation.onTermination = { _ in sensor.onReading = nil }
    }
}

let sensor = Sensor()
let readingStream = readings(from: sensor)
sensor.emit()

var received: [Double] = []
for await reading in readingStream {
    received.append(reading)
    if received.count == 2 { break }
}
print(received)   // [1.5, 2.5]

Common pitfalls

  • Blocking the cooperative pool with semaphores, wait(), or long synchronous work. Await instead, and move heavy CPU work off actors.
  • Actor reentrancy: assuming state is unchanged across an await inside an actor.
  • Forgetting that Task { } inherits the actor: a task started from @MainActor code runs on the main actor, so CPU-heavy work inside it blocks the UI.
  • Unstructured tasks that are never cancelled, outliving the screen that started them. Keep their handles and cancel them, or use structured APIs like SwiftUI’s .task modifier.
  • Overusing @unchecked Sendable to silence errors without real synchronization.

Interview questions

What’s the difference between suspending and blocking? A suspended function gives its thread back to the pool while it waits; a blocked thread sits idle. Swift concurrency suspends; blocking the cooperative pool can stall the whole app.

What’s the difference between async let, task groups, and Task { }? async let and task groups create structured child tasks bound to their scope, with automatic cancellation; Task { } creates an unstructured task that runs independently and inherits the current actor.

What is actor reentrancy, and why does it matter? At each await, an actor can run other calls. State checked before an await may be different afterwards, so update state before suspending or re-check after.

What does Sendable mean, and what changed in Swift 6? Sendable marks types safe to share across concurrency domains. Swift 6 language mode turns the checks into errors, guaranteeing data-race freedom at compile time, with region-based isolation and sending reducing false positives.

Summary

  • async functions suspend without blocking threads; await marks every suspension point, where other code may run.
  • Tasks run on a cooperative pool: never block it. Task { } starts unstructured work; async let and task groups run structured, cancellable child tasks.
  • Cancellation is cooperative; @TaskLocal values flow to child tasks.
  • Actors and @MainActor protect state, but actors are reentrant at each await.
  • Sendable, region-based isolation, and Swift 6 mode turn data races into compile errors; continuations and AsyncStream bridge older APIs.
entry.summary: For years, asynchronous Swift meant completion handlers, nested closures, and manual hops between dispatch queues, with data races found only by luck or by Thread Sanitizer. Swift concurrency replaces that with features built into the language: async/await for code that reads top to bottom, tasks for running work concurrently with structured cancellation, actors for protecting shared state, and, since Swift 6, a compiler that proves your code is free of data races. This article is a tour of the whole model, including the parts that trip people up.

entry.title: Macros in Swift
entry.content:
Swift macros, introduced in Swift 5.9, generate code at compile time. Write @Observable on a class, #Preview in a SwiftUI file, or #expect in a test, and the compiler expands it into ordinary Swift code that you can read, step through in the debugger, and reason about. Unlike C macros, Swift macros are type-checked, operate on syntax trees rather than text, and can’t silently change the meaning of the code around them. They’re also more work to write than a function, which is why knowing when to reach for one matters as much as knowing how.

Macros in Swift

Using macros

You’ve probably used macros already. There are two families.

Freestanding macros start with # and stand on their own, as an expression or a declaration:

import Foundation

struct Book {
    let title: String
    let pages: Int
}

let longBooks = #Predicate<Book> { book in
    book.pages > 300
}

let library = [Book(title: "Short", pages: 120), Book(title: "Long", pages: 640)]
print(try library.filter(longBooks).map(\.title))   // ["Long"]

#Predicate (Foundation, macOS 14 / iOS 17) turns a closure into a structured, inspectable predicate that SwiftData can translate into a database query. Other everyday examples: #Preview { … } in SwiftUI, #expect(…) and #require(…) in Swift Testing, and #warning("…").

Attached macros start with @ and are attached to a declaration, adding code to it or alongside it:

import Observation

@Observable
final class Counter {
    var count = 0
}

let counter = Counter()
counter.count += 1
print(counter.count)   // 1

Nothing is hidden: expanding a macro

In Xcode, right-click a macro and choose Expand Macro to see the generated code inline. Here’s (simplified) what @Observable produces for count:

// @ObservationIgnored private let _$observationRegistrar = ObservationRegistrar()
//
// @ObservationIgnored private var _count = 0
//
// var count: Int {
//     get {
//         access(keyPath: \.count)                  // record that someone read `count`
//         return _count
//     }
//     set {
//         withMutation(keyPath: \.count) {          // notify observers around the change
//             _count = newValue
//         }
//     }
// }
//
// extension Counter: Observable {}

The stored property moves to a private _count, and count becomes a computed property that reports reads and writes to an observation registrar. That’s how SwiftUI knows exactly which properties each view read, and redraws only views that depend on a changed property. (The exact expansion varies a little between compiler versions.)

This visibility is a big difference from runtime magic like swizzling: you can read exactly what runs, set breakpoints inside generated code, and see compiler errors pointing at it.

The roles a macro can play

Role Spelled What it can do
Expression #name(…) Produce a value, e.g. #Predicate, #expect
Declaration #name(…) Produce new declarations, e.g. #Preview
Peer @Name Add declarations next to the one it’s attached to
Accessor @Name Add get/set accessors to a property
Member @Name Add members to a type
Member attribute @Name Add attributes to a type’s members
Extension @Name Add an extension, e.g. a protocol conformance

A single macro can combine roles. @Observable is a member macro (adding the registrar), a member-attribute macro (marking each stored property @ObservationTracked, itself an accessor macro), and an extension macro (adding the Observable conformance).

How macros are built

A macro has two parts:

  1. A declaration, in your library, which defines the macro’s signature and points at its implementation.
  2. An implementation, in a separate compiler plugin, which receives the macro’s source code as a syntax tree and returns new syntax. Implementations use Apple’s SwiftSyntax package.

The canonical example, from Xcode’s macro template, is #stringify(x + y), which returns both the value and the source text that produced it.

The declaration:

@freestanding(expression)
public macro stringify<T>(_ value: T) -> (T, String) =
    #externalMacro(module: "MyMacrosPlugin", type: "StringifyMacro")

The implementation, which runs inside the compiler:

import SwiftCompilerPlugin
import SwiftSyntax
import SwiftSyntaxMacros

public struct StringifyMacro: ExpressionMacro {
    public static func expansion(
        of node: some FreestandingMacroExpansionSyntax,
        in context: some MacroExpansionContext
    ) -> ExprSyntax {
        guard let argument = node.arguments.first?.expression else {
            fatalError("compiler bug: the macro does not have any arguments")
        }
        return "(\(argument), \(literal: argument.description))"
    }
}

@main
struct MyMacrosPlugin: CompilerPlugin {
    let providingMacros: [Macro.Type] = [StringifyMacro.self]
}

And the call site:

// let (result, code) = #stringify(17 + 25)
// result == 42, code == "17 + 25"

The easiest way to start is File → New → Package → Swift Macro in Xcode, which sets up the declaration target, the plugin target, a client, and tests.

What the plugin sees, and what it doesn’t

A macro implementation only receives syntax: the source code it’s attached to, as a tree. It has no type information (it can’t ask “what’s the type of this expression?”) and can’t see other files or declarations elsewhere. It runs in a sandboxed process, with no file system or network access, and its output must depend only on its input. Those restrictions keep builds deterministic and macros predictable.

Validating input and reporting errors

Because a macro sees real syntax, it can check its input and emit compiler diagnostics. A URL macro, for example, can verify a string literal at compile time and return a non-optional URL, turning a runtime crash into a compile error with a clear message. In the implementation, that’s a thrown error or a call to context.diagnose(…) with a message, a location, and even suggested fix-its. No ordinary function can offer that.

Macros should also be hygienic: when they introduce helper variables, they use context.makeUniqueName(_:), so generated names can’t collide with names in the user’s code.

Testing macros

SwiftSyntax includes assertMacroExpansion, which compares a macro’s input with the exact source it should expand to, including expected diagnostics:

// assertMacroExpansion(
//     "#stringify(a + b)",
//     expandedSource: "(a + b, \"a + b\")",
//     macros: ["stringify": StringifyMacro.self]
// )

Macro tests are essential: a macro bug becomes a bug in every place the macro is used.

Macros vs. other tools

Need Best tool
Reusable logic around one property’s storage Property wrapper
Shared behavior across types Protocol with an extension
A computation A plain function, even a generic one
Boilerplate that must see a whole declaration (all properties, all cases) Macro
Checking a literal or argument at compile time Expression macro

Reach for a macro when the simpler tools genuinely can’t express what you need. @Observable is a macro rather than a property wrapper precisely because it has to rewrite every property of a type and add a conformance, which no property wrapper can do.

Costs to keep in mind

  • Build time. Macro packages depend on SwiftSyntax, a large library that has to be built along with your project, which noticeably slows clean builds.
  • Trust. A macro plugin runs code on your machine during the build. Xcode asks you to explicitly trust macros from packages for that reason.
  • Readability. One attribute can generate a lot of code. Keep macros’ behavior obvious, document it, and make the expansion easy to understand.
  • Debugging. Errors can point into generated code, so good diagnostics from the macro itself matter.

Interview questions

How do Swift macros differ from C preprocessor macros? Swift macros transform type-checked syntax trees in a sandboxed compiler plugin, their expansions are visible and debuggable, and they can’t change unrelated code. C macros are textual substitution with none of those guarantees.

What’s the difference between freestanding and attached macros? Freestanding macros (#name) produce an expression or declarations on their own; attached macros (@Name) modify or add to the declaration they’re attached to.

Why is @Observable a macro and not a property wrapper? It has to transform every stored property of a type and add a protocol conformance; property wrappers only control a single property’s storage.

What information does a macro implementation have? Only the syntax of its arguments and the declaration it’s attached to: no type information and no access to other files.

Summary

  • Macros generate Swift code at compile time; freestanding macros use #, attached macros use @.
  • Expansions are visible in Xcode, debuggable, and type-checked; @Observable’s expansion shows exactly how observation works.
  • Implementations live in sandboxed compiler plugins built with SwiftSyntax, see only syntax, and can emit real compiler diagnostics.
  • Test macros with assertMacroExpansion, and weigh their build-time and readability costs.
  • Use macros for boilerplate and compile-time checks that functions, protocols, and property wrappers can’t express.

entry.title: Nested Types in Swift
entry.content:
Some types only make sense in the context of another type. A playing card’s suit, a network client’s error, a view model’s state, a model’s coding keys: Swift lets you declare these types inside the type they belong to. Nested types keep related code together, avoid name clashes, express ownership, and make APIs read naturally at the call site. Since Swift 5.10, even protocols can be nested.

Nested Types in Swift

A first example

struct BlackjackCard {
    enum Suit: Character {
        case spades = "♠", hearts = "♡", diamonds = "♢", clubs = "♣"
    }

    enum Rank: Int {
        case two = 2, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten
        case jack, queen, king, ace

        struct Values {
            let first: Int
            let second: Int?
        }

        var values: Values {
            switch self {
            case .ace: Values(first: 1, second: 11)
            case .jack, .queen, .king: Values(first: 10, second: nil)
            default: Values(first: rawValue, second: nil)
            }
        }
    }

    let rank: Rank
    let suit: Suit

    var description: String {
        var output = "suit is \(suit.rawValue), value is \(rank.values.first)"
        if let second = rank.values.second {
            output += " or \(second)"
        }
        return output
    }
}

let theAceOfSpades = BlackjackCard(rank: .ace, suit: .spades)
print(theAceOfSpades.description)   // suit is ♠, value is 1 or 11

Types can nest as deeply as you need: Values lives inside Rank, which lives inside BlackjackCard.

Referring to nested types

Inside the outer type, you use the short name, Suit. Outside, you qualify it with the outer type:

let heartsSymbol = BlackjackCard.Suit.hearts.rawValue    // "♡"
let kingValues: BlackjackCard.Rank.Values = BlackjackCard.Rank.king.values
print(heartsSymbol, kingValues.first)                    // ♡ 10

Thanks to type inference, you rarely need the full name at call sites: BlackjackCard(rank: .ace, suit: .spades) already knows the types. Self.Suit also works inside the type, which is useful in protocol extensions and generic code.

Why nest?

1. Avoiding name clashes

Two types can each have their own State, Error, Configuration, or Style without prefixes:

struct LoginViewModel {
    enum State {
        case idle, submitting, failed(String)
    }
    var state = State.idle
}

struct CheckoutViewModel {
    enum State {
        case cart, paying, done
    }
    var state = State.cart
}

Compare that with top-level LoginViewModelState and CheckoutViewModelState: longer names, and nothing in the language tying them to their owners.

2. Expressing ownership

A nested type says “this belongs to that”. Reading APIClient.Error tells you exactly where the error comes from:

struct APIClient {
    enum Error: Swift.Error {
        case invalidURL
        case badStatus(Int)
    }

    func validate(status: Int) throws(APIClient.Error) {
        guard (200..<300).contains(status) else {
            throw .badStatus(status)
        }
    }
}

do {
    try APIClient().validate(status: 503)
} catch {
    print(error)   // badStatus(503)
}

Note the Swift.Error in the conformance: inside APIClient, the name Error now refers to the nested enum, so the standard protocol must be qualified with its module name. Shadowing like this is legal and common, but it’s worth knowing why the qualification is needed.

3. Scoping helpers with access control

A private nested type is invisible outside its parent, which is ideal for implementation details:

final class ImageLoader {
    private struct CacheEntry {
        let data: Data
        let date: Date
    }

    private var cache: [URL: CacheEntry] = [:]

    func store(_ data: Data, for url: URL) {
        cache[url] = CacheEntry(data: data, date: Date())
    }
}

The classic nested type: CodingKeys

The most common nested type in Swift code is CodingKeys, which customizes how Codable maps properties to JSON keys:

struct User: Codable {
    let id: Int
    let displayName: String

    enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey {
        case id
        case displayName = "display_name"
    }
}

let json = #"{"id": 1, "display_name": "Sam"}"#
let decoded = try JSONDecoder().decode(User.self, from: Data(json.utf8))
print(decoded.displayName)   // Sam

Codable looks for a nested type with exactly that name, which shows how nested types can act as a convention between a type and the frameworks that use it.

Nested protocols (Swift 5.10)

Since Swift 5.10, protocols can be nested inside non-generic types. That’s perfect for delegate protocols, which belong to the type that calls them:

final class TableView {
    protocol Delegate: AnyObject {
        func didSelect(row: Int)
    }

    weak var delegate: Delegate?

    func tap(row: Int) {
        delegate?.didSelect(row: row)
    }
}

final class SettingsScreen: TableView.Delegate {
    func didSelect(row: Int) {
        print("Selected row \(row)")
    }
}

let table = TableView()
let settings = SettingsScreen()
table.delegate = settings
table.tap(row: 2)   // Selected row 2

TableView.Delegate reads better than a top-level TableViewDelegate, and the protocol lives right next to the code that uses it.

Nesting in extensions

You can add nested types in an extension, which helps keep a large type organized, or add helper types to a type you don’t own:

extension BlackjackCard {
    enum Color {
        case red, black
    }

    var color: Color {
        switch suit {
        case .hearts, .diamonds: .red
        case .spades, .clubs: .black
        }
    }
}

print(theAceOfSpades.color)   // black

Nested types and generics

A type nested inside a generic type can use the outer type’s parameters:

struct LinkedList<Element> {
    final class Node {
        let value: Element          // uses the outer generic parameter
        var next: Node?
        init(value: Element) { self.value = value }
    }

    private(set) var head: Node?

    mutating func prepend(_ value: Element) {
        let node = Node(value: value)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    }
}

var list = LinkedList<String>()
list.prepend("world")
list.prepend("hello")
print(list.head?.value ?? "")   // hello

LinkedList<String>.Node and LinkedList<Int>.Node are different types, each specialized for its element type.

Namespaces with caseless enums

Swift has no namespace keyword, but an enum with no cases can’t be instantiated, which makes it a clean container for related constants and helpers:

enum Constants {
    enum API {
        static let baseURL = "https://api.example.com"
        static let timeout = 30.0
    }

    enum Layout {
        static let padding = 16.0
    }
}

print(Constants.API.baseURL)

A caseless enum is preferred over a struct for this, because a struct could accidentally be instantiated: Constants().

Under the hood

Nesting is purely about naming and scope. A nested type has no hidden reference to an instance of its outer type (unlike inner classes in Java), and it doesn’t make the outer type larger. BlackjackCard.Suit is an ordinary enum whose full name, in symbols and in String(reflecting:), includes its parent: MyApp.BlackjackCard.Suit.

When not to nest

Deep nesting makes names long and code hard to scan. If a type is useful on its own, or used by many unrelated types, it probably deserves to be top-level. A good rule: nest when the inner type genuinely belongs to the outer one, and its name only makes sense next to the parent’s.

Interview questions

Does a nested type have access to an instance of its outer type? No. Nesting only affects naming and scope; the nested type has no hidden reference to an outer instance.

Why write Swift.Error inside a type that declares its own Error? The nested Error shadows the standard library protocol inside that type, so the protocol must be qualified with its module.

Can protocols be nested? Since Swift 5.10, inside non-generic types, which is great for delegate protocols like TableView.Delegate.

How do you create a namespace in Swift? With a caseless enum holding static members and nested types.

Summary

  • Declare types inside other types when they only make sense in that context; use the short name inside and Outer.Inner outside.
  • Nesting avoids name clashes, expresses ownership, and combines well with private; CodingKeys is the classic example.
  • Protocols can be nested in non-generic types since Swift 5.10.
  • Types nested in generic types can use the outer type’s parameters.
  • Caseless enums work as namespaces; nesting has no runtime cost and no hidden outer reference.
